title: What If You Fell Into Lava? You Wouldn't Sink, and That's the Problem

scenes.text: What if you fell into lava? You wouldn't sink. That's the bad news.
Every movie gets this wrong. Lava is about 3,100 kilograms per cubic metre. You are about 1,010. Three times lighter than the thing you're falling into.
So you don't slide under like a character in a film. You land on top, like a cork on water.
And it isn't liquid the way water is. Lava resists flowing 100,000 to a million times more than water. Think peanut butter, not soup.
Which leaves you lying on a surface of 1,100 degrees Celsius. Four times hotter than an oven on broil.
Geoscientist Erik Klemetti puts it simply: molten lava is nothing like water. You don't disappear into it. You burn on top of it. Still want to visit the volcano?

description:
What if you fell into lava? Geoscientist Erik Klemetti calculates that basaltic lava has a density of about 3,100 kg per cubic metre against roughly 1,010 for a human, so a person would float on the surface rather than sink; lava is also 100,000 to over a million times more viscous than water, closer to peanut butter than to liquid.
At around 1,100 to 1,200 degrees Celsius, roughly four times the temperature of an oven on broil, the heat would set a person on fire on the surface, which is why both Live Science and Discover conclude the Hollywood sinking scene is wrong.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: Klemetti's at-home version: a styrofoam figure dropped into motor oil. It floats, every time. Which movie scene should science ruin next? Drop your own what-if below.
